cards.topic: Team movement dynamics across the field
cards.promptSummary: Analyze by team phase, then unit and player. Keep width, depth, line distances, centroid, ball-side shift, weak side, between-line position, overload, rest defence and recovery run distinct. A team shift needs multiple aligned observations and opponent context; a single frame is a snapshot, not a movement trend. Compare measured change with possession/phase and opponent response. State coverage and missing players. Event-only feeds cannot prove off-ball movement, shape, compactness, body orientation, velocity or intent.
mechanisms: Describe team behavior by phase: settled build-up, progression, final-third attack, defensive organization, pressing, transition after regain, and transition after loss.
Distinguish nominal starting formation from phase-dependent shape, player role, and a specific tactical mechanism. A shape can change with the ball, opponent, score, personnel, and restart.

Useful spatial summaries include team width, team length, centroid, between-line distance, line height, local density, inter-player spacing, and ball-to-block distance; every metric needs a defined player set and coordinate reference.

Team movement is interaction: compare the team's movement with ball movement and opponent response. A shift toward the ball may preserve compactness, create weak-side space, or be a retreat; context determines which is supported.

Track width/depth occupation, support angles, passing lanes, overloads, runs beyond, third-player actions, rest defence, and recovery runs as distinct mechanisms rather than synonyms for attacking or defending well.
requiredEvidence: Use time-synchronized tracking with validated coordinate units, pitch dimensions, axes, attack direction per team/period, player identity/team mapping, timestamps and stated frame coverage for spatial/shape claims.
Use ordered source events with original IDs, sequence, period and match-time semantics to describe event sequences; do not reconstruct missing time or movement between sparse frames.
State which players/lines are observed and missing. A single frame supports a snapshot, not a coordinated movement trend.
analysisSteps: Fix match revision, selected time and sequence watermark; normalize coordinates to the attacking team's direction only after the source convention is validated.
Establish phase and possession from canonical events, then identify the ball zone and relevant team/opponent units.
Compare multiple aligned frames to describe movement direction and change; quantify a metric only with an explicit definition and coverage window.
Separate measured movement from role/shape interpretation; offer a plausible alternative when evidence supports more than one reading.
Close with an outcome only if the subsequent selected-time evidence documents it.
limitations: Event-only data cannot establish off-ball movement, collective compactness, body orientation, line height or pitch control.
Unverified coordinates or timestamps block metres, speed, direction, duration and before/after movement claims.
Do not infer a coach's instruction, player intention, tactical quality or causality from synchronized movement alone.

cards.promptSummary: Before spatial claims, require validated pitch dimensions, coordinate unit/origin/axes, period-specific attack direction, identity/team mapping, time alignment, frame cadence, missingness and versioned metric definitions. A local overload is counted in a declared zone and time; a passing lane needs origin, receiver and intervening defenders. Use the least specific defensible wording when calibration is missing. Never convert unknown 0–100 coordinates to metres or estimate velocity from sparse frames.
mechanisms: A zone is a declared partition of the pitch; name the partition/version before describing central, half-space, wide, defensive or final-third locations.
Distances need a known unit and pitch calibration. Angles and left/right need known axes and attack orientation. Reflecting the pitch for the opposite attack direction must preserve football meaning.
A local overload is a counted numerical or positional advantage in a declared area and time. Global player counts or possession percentages do not establish a local overload.
A passing lane is a geometric and temporal path with an origin, receiver and intervening defenders; event success alone does not show whether the lane was open or intentionally created.
State space/time coverage: observed players, sample interval, missing frames, tracking interpolation, and whether each value is measured or derived.
requiredEvidence: Validated coordinate origin, axes, units, pitch dimensions, orientation and team-relative direction.
Identity-bound, timestamp-aligned player and ball positions with missingness and sampling metadata.
Versioned definitions for zones, lines, compactness, overload and any spatial thresholds.
analysisSteps: Check source semantics and mapping status before calculating spatial measures.
Select a time window no later than the requested selected time and list the exact frame IDs used.
Define the players, zone and metric, including threshold and units; expose uncertainty and missing coverage.
Use the least specific defensible phrase when calibration is incomplete: event progression rather than metres, snapshot rather than movement, proximity rather than pressure.
limitations: Do not convert 0–100 values to metres or assume origin/orientation without an authoritative source dictionary.
Do not estimate velocity from sparse frames or fill missing players with invented positions.
Do not report expected threat, expected goals, pitch control or numerical advantage without validated models and coverage.

cards.promptSummary: A 2v1 is a local, time-specific relationship: two eligible attackers versus one relevant defender in a defined area, with nearby cover checked. The carrier may commit the defender and pass, attack space if the defender delays, combine through a third player, or recycle if cover closes the route. Distinguish overlap (outside/beyond) from underlap (inside); a third-player combination needs the intermediate action. Track defender engage/delay/screen/show and the next evidenced outcome. Require aligned calibrated positions and IDs; events alone do not prove the 2v1 or what a player should have done.
mechanisms: A 2v1 is a local, time-specific relationship: two eligible attackers can act against one relevant defender in a defined corridor/zone. State whether the ball carrier is included in the two and what defensive support is outside the local picture.

The ball carrier's choices are carry to commit the defender, pass to the free teammate, or hold/return if the defender delays. The best choice depends on distance, pressure, angle, support, goal/space, and defender cover; the model may describe options, not assert the player's unobserved intent.

An overlap is an outside run beyond the ball carrier; an underlap is an inside run. A third-player combination requires the ball to pass through an intermediate player before reaching the third; do not infer these from a final pass alone.

The defender can engage the carrier, delay and protect depth, block the pass lane, show play outside/inside, or wait for cover. Describe only the observed response and avoid declaring a mistake from outcome alone.

Evaluate the sequence: initial numerical relation → carrier action → defender commitment/containment → pass or carry → receiver's next action → documented result (progress, cross, shot, regain, turnover or no outcome).
requiredEvidence: Aligned positions for the ball, both attackers, the relevant defender, nearby cover defenders and target space at the interaction time.
Validated identity/team mapping, coordinates/orientation, frame cadence and event timestamps; use events to confirm pass/carry and outcome.
For event-only feeds, require explicit canonical local-overload evidence. Otherwise say the event sequence does not prove a 2v1.
analysisSteps: Define the corridor/zone, time and participants; check whether a covering defender changes the true local count.
Record carrier, support-runner and defender positions/angles only if observed; distinguish a static snapshot from changing movement.
Identify the defender's choice (engage, delay, screen, show) and the attacker's observable action.
Describe the tactical trade-off: commit defender to release teammate, carry into space if defender holds, or recycle if the lane closes.
Report the evidenced outcome and whether the defender's action preserved cover; do not rank decision quality without context.
limitations: A pass followed by a cross does not prove an earlier 2v1, defender commitment, or deliberate overload.
Sparse tracking can miss the cover defender, offside line, body orientation, pressure or the timing that makes the advantage real.
Do not claim the player should have passed, dribbled or shot as a factual conclusion; phrase options conditionally.

cards.promptSummary: A substitution proves personnel changed, not motive, fatigue, injury, instruction, role or formation. Potential effects include lane coverage, width/depth, pressing/recovery, progression, aerial outlet, transition balance and restart roles. Pin the event and active roster; compare defined pre/post windows on the same measures and state selected-time limits. Control for score, opponent changes, dismissals, stoppages, possession and small samples. Describe association ('after the change, X was observed'), not causation. Validate period and added-time semantics before saying 'last minute'.
mechanisms: A substitution event proves only that one player left and another entered at a recorded time, subject to source validity. Tactical role, formation change, instruction, fitness state and motive are separate claims.

Possible mechanisms include fresh running capacity, a like-for-like role, a role conversion, adding/removing a forward or defender, changing pressing coverage, protecting a channel, increasing width/height, or managing a restart. Treat these as hypotheses until observable post-change behavior supports one.

A late substitution can alter pressing intensity, transition speed, defensive line, possession outlet, aerial matchups, set-piece assignments and game-state risk—but only if those variables are actually observed.

Assess pre/post windows with comparable state: score, period, possession share, opponent behavior, red cards, restart frequency and time remaining. A substitution coinciding with a change does not establish it caused the change.
Separate immediate settling-in effects from sustained shape: inspect first actions and a later stable window, but do not compare beyond the selected-time cutoff.
requiredEvidence: Canonical substitution event, outgoing/incoming player identities, team, source time/period, and active roster before/after.
Validated role/position labels or time-aligned tracking before and after; identify changed coverage and observed tasks rather than inferring a coach's instruction.
A stated comparison window and game-state controls. Small samples and stoppages must be reported.
analysisSteps: Pin the exact substitution event and selected-time revision; reject any post-substitution evidence later than the selected time.
Describe the personnel fact, then list evidence-supported role/shape differences; if role evidence is absent, stop at personnel change.
Compare a defined pre-window with a post-window, aligning time, possession/phase and opponent context where possible.
Check alternative explanations: score state, opponent substitution, dismissal, injury stoppage, tactical change by opponent, sample variance.
Use association language: 'after the change, observed X'; reserve causal wording for a validated evaluation design.
limitations: Do not infer fatigue, injury, manager intent, player quality, formation change or a substitution's success from the event alone.
A few post-change events cannot establish that the substitute caused a tactical improvement or deterioration.
Late clocks and stoppage-time labels are provider-specific; validate semantics before claiming 'last minute' or elapsed duration.

cards.topic: Late-game fouls, stoppages and tactical-foul hypotheses
cards.promptSummary: Separate recorded foul, advantage/whistle, restart, card and next action. A tactical-foul label is a cautious interpretation only when a verified foul interrupts an evidenced transition; late timing alone does not prove deliberate time-wasting, instruction or cynicism. Pin clock/period, score, restart location and cards. Describe observed football consequences neutrally; do not advise fouling, adjudicate referee correctness or infer that the foul changed the result. Validate added-time semantics before 'last minute'.
mechanisms: First distinguish an observed foul, a foul decision, advantage, card, restart location and subsequent restart outcome. These are related but different facts.
A tactical foul is an interpretation that a player deliberately stopped an opponent's transition; a late foul is not automatically tactical, time-wasting, cynical, instructed or strategic.

Potential context includes transition speed, opponent numerical advantage, field zone, nearby cover, score, period, remaining time, card state and foul/restart pattern. Describe only available evidence.
Foul consequences may include direct/indirect free kick, penalty, card, dismissal risk, set-piece delivery and lost playing time. Do not infer expected danger without a validated model.
Repeated restarts or slow restarts can be consistent with time management, injury, referee procedure or tactical rhythm; intent needs external authoritative evidence.
requiredEvidence: Canonical foul event with offender/team, opponent action, source time/period, location if validated, restart/advantage and card events if present.
Transition evidence before the foul to describe what it interrupted; a foul event by itself does not establish a counterattack.
Validated regulation/stoppage-time semantics before making claims about the final minute or remaining time.
analysisSteps: Describe the foul and restart as recorded, preserving the original event ID and match-time meaning.
If supported, describe the phase before contact (settled attack, counterattack, press escape, set piece); do not assume tactical intent.
State the relevant match state and disciplinary context only from the selected canonical packet.
Explain the tactical trade-off conditionally: the defending team may have stopped a transition but conceded a restart; identify what is known and unknown.
Separate event effect (play stopped, restart awarded) from consequence (shot, card, goal, time lost) and report only observed downstream events.
limitations: Do not advise a player to foul, celebrate dangerous conduct, or claim a manager ordered it.
Do not call it deliberate time-wasting or tactical cynicism based only on late timing or repeated fouls.
Do not assess referee correctness, severity, card threshold or foul location without authoritative adjudication data.

cards.promptSummary: Describe whether a team builds short, progresses through a line, goes around pressure, plays over it, switches play, or attacks directly. These are route descriptions, not quality judgments. Check support angles, receiver orientation and opponent pressure only when observed. A switch can move the defensive block and create a far-side option, but the resulting space/overload must be measured or explicitly evidenced. Distinguish possession from progression and progression from chance creation.
mechanisms: Build-up may use goalkeeper/defenders as spare players, attract pressure, then find a free player; do not infer a designed press bait from a pass sequence alone.
Progression can go through, around, or over an opponent unit, or switch the attack to the far side; define the opponent line and sequence.
Support triangles, third-player actions, rotations, overlaps, underlaps, width and depth are distinct mechanisms that require role/position evidence.
Direct play is not synonymous with aimless play: the target, second-ball support, territory, retention and next action determine what is evidenced.
requiredEvidence: Ordered pass/carry events with validated team possession, sequence and time.
Validated coordinates and tracking to describe line access, support angles, receiving orientation, space or opponent movement.
Clearly distinguish source facts from a detector-derived route/line-break label.
analysisSteps: Identify the phase and pressure context.
Describe the route and intended/evidenced receiver without assuming coach intent.
Track whether the action bypassed an opponent unit, retained possession, progressed territory or created a chance.
Name the opponent response and any unknown spatial context.
limitations: A completed forward pass alone does not prove a line break, tactical control or a purposeful build-up plan.
Do not claim a player could see or intended a pass without sensory/intent evidence.

cards.topic: Final-third creation, box occupation and finishing actions
cards.promptSummary: Analyze final-third attacks as separate stages: entry, defensive-line response, wide/central creation, box occupation, delivery/cutback, shot and rebound/second ball. Width/depth, an overlap, half-space access, crossing lane and coordinated runs need calibrated player evidence. Count box attackers and rest-defence cover only from time-aligned positions. A cross, entry or shot is not automatically a high-quality chance; do not infer xG or danger without a validated model and shot features.
mechanisms: An entry can be a pass, carry, cross or restart; name the recorded action and destination.
Wide attacks may use overlap/underlap, isolate a defender, cross early, reach the byline, or cut the ball back; do not presume which was intended.
Box occupation includes near-post, central, far-post and edge support roles; distinguish observed locations/runs from assigned roles.
Rest defence balances numbers committed forward with protection against the counter; state the observed players and spaces rather than a quality grade.
requiredEvidence: Canonical attack/shot events, source IDs and selected-time sequence.
Validated tracking for box runs, delivery lanes, defender shape, cross/cutback zone and rest-defence cover.
A validated chance-quality model and inputs before reporting xG or chance quality.
analysisSteps: Locate the final-third entry and identify the next action sequence.
Describe defender movement and attacker runs only if the frames show them.
Separate delivery, first contact, shot and outcome.
State whether the packet documents a shot/goal or ends before the result.
limitations: Do not infer the intended target or quality of a cross from where the ball ended up.
Do not label danger, control or expected goals from possession, field location or outcome alone.

cards.promptSummary: Start a transition at a verified regain or loss. In attack, trace first action, forward option, support runs, opponent recovery and terminal outcome; in defence, trace immediate counterpress/delay, central protection and recovery. A counterattack requires evidenced rapid forward exploitation, not merely a long pass or later goal. Rest defence is the attacking side's observed protection behind the ball before loss. Require validated clock, possession and tracking before speed, imbalance, space or numerical claims.
mechanisms: After a regain, options include attack space directly, carry, combine quickly, or retain and reorganize; describe the observed choice.
After a loss, immediate pressure may aim to regain, delay may allow teammates to recover, or players may retreat to protect the goal.
The opponent simultaneously transitions to defend; analyze both teams' positions and decisions as an interaction.
Rest-defence shape can secure central routes, protect depth, and prepare a counterpress or recovery, but roles cannot be inferred from a single outcome.
requiredEvidence: Canonical possession change and ordered actions with valid clock/period semantics.
Time-aligned tracking for runners, defenders, exposed space, recovery route and rest-defence positions.
Coverage window long enough to capture the transition and any terminal outcome.
analysisSteps: Mark the possession-change event and participating teams.
Trace the first forward/defensive action and support/cover movement.
Record whether the opponent was organized, recovering or attacking only when observed.
End at the selected-time cutoff; list missing links and avoid causal claims.
limitations: Do not call it a counterattack without evidence of speed/direct exploitation and opponent disorganization.
Do not infer fatigue or poor rest defence from a single counter chance.

cards.promptSummary: Classify the restart first, then separate setup, delivery, first contact, second ball, clearance/retention and final outcome. Corner/free-kick routines may use short options, near/far/central zones, blockers, decoy runs and recycled delivery, but intent and assignments require authoritative evidence. Defensive teams may use zonal, player-to-player or mixed marking; a frame alone rarely proves scheme. Require canonical restart/event and calibrated tracking. One event cannot establish routine quality or conversion rate.
mechanisms: Attacking: delivery to a zone, short restart, screen/block, movement to separate markers, second-phase recycle, or protection against a counter.
Defending: protect goal/space, track runners, contest first contact, clear danger and organize the next phase.
Throw-ins, free kicks, corners, penalties and goal kicks have different restart rules and tactical contexts.
A second ball is a distinct contest after a clearance or first contact and needs a subsequent possession/event observation.
requiredEvidence: Canonical restart type, event ID, team, time, delivery/action and restart outcome.
Tracking with verified orientation and player identity for movement, marking, target zones and second-ball shape.
Defined sample and denominator for rates or team-level set-piece tendencies.
analysisSteps: Confirm restart classification and location semantics.
Describe setup/delivery only from evidence; distinguish observed movement from assumed design.
Follow first and second contact to the documented outcome.
Mention counter-protection only if the relevant players/space are shown.
limitations: Do not invent a routine, target player, marking assignment or coach instruction.
Do not treat a retained attack as a successful set piece without an explicitly defined outcome measure.

cards.topic: Game state, risk and in-match adjustments
cards.promptSummary: Fix score, period, clock, player availability and possession at the selected time. Tactical risk may change with game state, but a scoreline does not reveal intent. Describe observable changes in directness, width, pressing, line height, substitutions or restart tempo only with evidence and a defined comparison. Separate an observed adjustment from the hypothesis explaining it. Never predict results or prescribe a specific formation/substitution without squad, role and validated model context.
mechanisms: A team may protect depth, press higher, attack more directly, retain possession, overload a zone or make personnel changes as the state changes; these are alternative hypotheses.
The opponent may also alter approach, and red cards, injuries, timeouts/restarts and competition rules change the context.
A useful comparison aligns periods/windows and reports sample size, possession/phase mix, score, personnel and opponent changes.
Risk is multi-dimensional: forward commitment, spacing behind the ball, transition exposure, set-piece coverage and time remaining.
requiredEvidence: Canonical score/revision and validated period/elapsed-time/added-time semantics.
Ordered events for substitutions, dismissals, restarts, attacks and possession; tracking for shape/commitment.
Defined pre/post or state comparison and known confounders.
analysisSteps: Pin the exact selected state.
Describe the observed behavior before offering an interpretation.
Compare only equivalent evidence windows and identify confounders.
Use conditional tactical options rather than claims about what a coach intended or should do.
limitations: Do not infer urgency, time-wasting, risk appetite or manager intent from score/time alone.
Do not forecast score, win probability or optimal substitution without a separately validated model.

cards.topic: Pressing, block movement and defensive response
cards.promptSummary: Separate high press, mid/low block, isolated pressure, counterpress and recovery. Explain trigger → pressure → cover/support → opponent response → regain/escape → next action. Collective shifting needs multiple aligned player/line observations; compactness has separate horizontal and vertical dimensions. A trap needs an evidenced route constraint and opponent response. A regain after pressure is a sequence, not proof of cause. Event-only data cannot establish cover shadows, block shape, coordination, intensity or line height.
mechanisms: Separate high press, mid-block, low block, counterpress and isolated pressure; each describes a different phase or field position and needs operational criteria.
A collective press involves a trigger, pressure on the ball, supporting pressure/cover, constrained exits and an opponent response. One close defender is not proof of collective pressing.
Block movement can shift toward the ball, drop to protect depth, step up to compress space, or split while chasing a runner. Confirm coordinated movement across multiple lines and frames.
A trap is not just a location: identify the intended route constraint and the opponent's evidenced action. A regain after pressure is associated in sequence, not automatically caused by pressure.
After a turnover, distinguish counterpress to regain near the loss from recovery defending toward own goal; link each to the documented possession state.
requiredEvidence: Ordered possession/event sequence and outcome; team-relative pitch orientation for high/mid/low location.
Time-aligned player locations and adequate tracking coverage for collective pressure, cover shadows, block shift and line distances.
Validated clock and spatial thresholds before calling a response immediate, close, compact or high.
analysisSteps: Establish possession and phase, then name the observable trigger or explicitly say none is visible.
Describe ball pressure and supporting shape only to the extent shown by evidence.
Follow the opponent response and classify the outcome: retained, escaped, forced backward/long, lost or unknown.
Describe regain and exploitation as later stages with their own evidence IDs; do not compress the sequence into causal certainty.
limitations: Event-only data cannot prove cover shadows, pressing intensity, shape, coordination or line height.
Do not infer a manager's pressing plan, player effort or tactical success from a detector label alone.
Incomplete frames, identity gaps and period/time ambiguity weaken sequence-level conclusions.

cards.topic: Formation, role and phase-dependent team shape
cards.promptSummary: Require a verified lineup to name starting formation. Infer dynamic phase shape only from repeated, aligned tracking with validated IDs, coordinates, phase and coverage; a single frame or event-only feed is insufficient. State window and uncertainty.
mechanisms: A formation label such as 4-3-3 or 4-2-3-1 is a compact description of a nominal starting arrangement. Provider and analyst conventions can differ on which line a wide or advanced midfielder belongs to; state the convention and use an authoritative lineup where available.

Team shape is a time-varying distribution of players in relation to teammates, opponents, ball, goal and phase. It can be asymmetric and change during one possession; the shape name is a summary, not a complete tactical explanation.

Distinguish the verified starting formation from observed in-possession structure, out-of-possession block, pressing shape, transition/recovery shape, restart organization and individual role. A team can use different structures across these situations without a substitution.

Common illustrative transformations include a nominal back four becoming a three-player build-up line when one full-back stays deeper and the other advances, or wide players dropping into a midfield line out of possession. These are possible mechanisms only; confirm actual player locations and roles before applying them.

Assess occupation and balance: width on both sides, depth behind the last line, central and half-space access, vertical staggering, distances between units, players behind the ball, cover for advanced players and exposed counter lanes. Do not treat a fixed count of players in a lane as proof of control.

Formation and shape interact with opponent pressure, ball location, score, personnel, restarts and game state. Compare like phases and windows before describing a change; a single snapshot cannot show a transformation or its cause.
requiredEvidence: A canonical starting lineup/role source and a documented notation convention for a named starting formation.

For observed phase shape: time-aligned player identities, team affiliations, calibrated pitch coordinates, attack direction, phase/possession labels, selected period/time window and player/frame coverage.

For a claim that shape changed: multiple synchronized observations before and after a defined trigger, with sufficient coverage of the relevant unit; report alternative explanations and missing players.
For role, pressing, build-up or rest-defence interpretations: evidence of player locations and interactions with the ball, opponent and teammates; event-only feeds do not supply off-ball structure.
analysisSteps: Fix match revision, period, selected time and sequence cutoff. Establish whether the question concerns starting lineup, settled possession, defensive organization, pressing, transition or a restart.
Confirm the source formation/role convention. If no authoritative lineup exists, do not name a starting formation from event destinations or player reputations.
Validate coordinate units, pitch axes, attack direction, identity mapping, timestamps and coverage before analyzing shape. Normalize sides only with a validated convention.

Describe the observed arrangement at team and unit scales: line relationships, width/depth, staggering, ball-relative occupation and protection behind the ball. Separate directly observed locations from any derived clustering or inferred role.
Use a window of repeated, comparable observations to describe a phase structure or change. State the phase, window, coverage and confidence; compare equivalent contexts when possible.

Connect the structure to a possible tactical function only if the evidence shows relevant opponent pressure, passing options, space, progression, defensive response or transition outcome. Present alternatives where plausible.
limitations: Do not infer a formation, player role, instruction or tactical intent from a club reputation, a coach name, a single frame, an event-only feed or a model-generated summary.
A named formation is not a performance rating and does not establish width, compactness, control, balance or suitability by itself.
Uncalibrated coordinates, missing identities, unknown attack direction, sparse frames or incomparable phases block strong spatial and shape conclusions.
Do not infer causation from a correlation between a shape and an outcome; score, opponent behavior, dismissals, substitutions and sample coverage can confound comparisons.

cards.topic: Formation advantages through defensive-attacking player combinations
cards.promptSummary: Formation is a starting reference, not a fixed shape. In 4-3-3, pivot plus two 8s connect a back four to three forwards; a full-back, winger and 8 can rotate overlap, underlap or hold width while the far side/pivot protect counters. 4-2-3-1 pairs complementary pivots behind a 10 and wide forwards; 4-4-2 pairs strikers and midfield banks but can be outnumbered centrally. 4-2-2-2 overloads central lanes and relies on full-backs for width. 3-5-2 pairs wing-backs, three centre-backs and two forwards; 3-4-3 stretches width but its midfield two can be overloaded. 4-1-4-1 screens central space but may isolate its lone striker. Every advantage has a space/cover trade-off; apply only after verifying actual roles, phase, opponent and evidence.
mechanisms: In a 4-3-3, the single pivot can offer a build-up outlet and screen central counters while two 8s connect to the wide forwards and striker. A full-back can overlap outside a winger, underlap inside, or hold the deeper line; each choice changes width, passing angles and protection behind the ball.

The 4-2-3-1 can combine a back four with two pivots of complementary functions (for example, one holding while the other advances), a 10 between lines, and two wide forwards. The 10 links the midfield to the striker; the pivots can cover full-backs or receive under pressure. If both pivots stay flat, the 10/striker may become disconnected; if both advance, central counter protection can weaken.

A 4-4-2 can pair one forward who pressures or pins a centre-back with a partner who supports, drops or threatens depth. Two midfield banks can protect central routes and shift together; wide midfielders must coordinate with full-backs so one engages while another provides cover. The shape may concede a central numerical disadvantage against three central midfielders unless a forward or wide midfielder adjusts.

A 3-5-2 can use three centre-backs to support build-up and cover wide centre-back channels, wing-backs for width and recovery, a central midfielder to screen, and two forwards to combine or occupy separate defenders. The far wing-back can provide weak-side width or a back-post run; the near wing-back needs cover when advancing.

A 3-4-3 adds a front three for high pressure and wide/inside threats while wing-backs support the attack. Its two central midfielders need coordinated distances and help from a dropping forward or stepping wide centre-back against a central overload; wing-back space behind is a transition risk.

A 4-2-2-2 places two narrow attacking midfielders behind two forwards, creating short central combinations and multiple links around the ball. Full-backs often supply outside width, so the pivots and centre-backs need a clear cover rotation if both advance; opponents may target the vacated wide channels.

A 4-1-4-1 can layer a holding midfielder in front of the centre-backs and a midfield line that supports pressure or closes central access. The lone striker can screen a pivot and lead the press, but needs nearby midfield support or an outlet run to avoid isolation after a regain.

Wide-unit synergy depends on staggered options: winger holds width or attacks inside, full-back overlaps/underlaps or stays, and an 8 offers a bounce pass or third-player run. If all three occupy the same lane, they can crowd each other; if the full-back advances without cover, the opponent can counter into that channel.

Front-pair/front-three synergy can pin a defensive line, threaten depth, check between lines, press a return pass or create a third-player run. These are alternative roles that players exchange; a formation number does not establish who performs them.

A balanced attack needs a rest-defence relationship: centre-backs, pivot(s), and a far-side full-back/wing-back decide who secures the center and channels behind advancing players. More players ahead can improve box occupation while increasing exposure after a turnover; assess both sides of the trade-off.
requiredEvidence: A verified lineup and notation convention for the nominal formation; do not infer it from team reputation or event locations.
Time-aligned player locations and identity/role evidence across the relevant phase to establish actual lines, rotations, width, depth and which defenders/midfielders/forwards combine.
Evidence of opponent structure/pressure and the subsequent action before claiming that a combination created a free player, overload, passing route, progression or chance.
For rest-defence or transition-risk claims, observed players behind/around the ball at the loss and the opponent response after the turnover.
analysisSteps: Name the nominal setup only from verified lineup evidence; state that the notation describes a starting reference.
Identify phase, ball location and opponent arrangement. Use repeated synchronized frames for role/shape relationships, not a single frame alone.
Trace the relevant unit links: centre-back/pivot, pivot/8/10, full-back/winger/8, or forward pair/third runner. Describe the observed movement and available support.
State the possible advantage and its matching risk together (for example, width gained by an advancing full-back and space exposed behind).
Compare the opponent response and outcome using evidence IDs. Avoid rating a formation in isolation or claiming causality from a short sequence.
limitations: These formations are illustrative coaching models, not fixed player duties or guaranteed advantages. Real structures are asymmetric and change by phase, opponent, score, personnel and instructions.
A nominal formation alone cannot establish player quality, suitability, tactical intent, success, spacing, local overload or defensive cover.
Event-only data cannot establish off-ball combinations or rest-defence shape. Unknown coordinates, timestamps, attack direction, identity or frame coverage block spatial conclusions.
Treat positional “advantages” as conditional mechanisms. Do not conclude the listed shape caused a goal, prevented a counter or was superior without a suitable comparison and evidence.

cards.promptSummary: Compare the actual phase shapes, not just formation labels. Look for local overloads, spare defenders, press-cover links and weak-side space. A role adjustment can solve one problem while exposing another; compare the opponent response and transition cover before calling it an advantage.
mechanisms: A nominal 4-3-3 against a 4-4-2 may offer a third central midfielder against a pair, while the 4-4-2 can use two forwards to press or pin centre-backs and wide midfielders to protect full-backs. Test whether the nominal spare can receive/use the ball and whether the opponent closes that route.

A 4-2-3-1 facing a 4-3-3 may use its 10 between the opponent pivot and defence, but the opponent three can outnumber the double pivot. A wide forward dropping to help can restore numbers while reducing the counter-attacking outlet.

A back three against a front two can create an extra first-line build-up player; the opponent may instead press wing-backs or use a midfielder to jump to the spare centre-back. A wing-back held high can pin a full-back, but exposes the channel if the wide centre-back cannot cover.

An in-game adjustment may be a role/height/side change inside the same nominal formation: a winger drops to the midfield line, a full-back stays to make a back three, a pivot steps forward, or a forward screens a pivot. Describe what changed and the space opened elsewhere.

When the opponent overloads a flank, possible responses include shifting a midfielder wide, narrowing the far-side winger, having a full-back engage earlier, or changing the press direction. Each changes central cover, far-side access, or the outlet after a regain.
Compare score, personnel, dismissal, phase, ball location and opponent behavior before and after any adjustment. Do not infer a coach instruction from the resulting shape alone.
requiredEvidence: Verified lineup and formation notation if naming a nominal shape.
Repeated, time-aligned player locations, identities, phase, ball/opponent locations and coverage for observed matchup or role change.
Evidence of the opponent response and next action before claiming an overload, spare player, free route or successful adjustment.
analysisSteps: State nominal lineup formation only when sourced; otherwise describe the observed phase shape.
Identify the phase, local unit, relevant players and opponent arrangement.
Count local options and cover using an explicitly bounded zone/time; note defenders who can recover.
Describe the adjustment as observed, then name the space gained and space conceded as hypotheses.
Compare opponent response and subsequent outcome with evidence IDs; offer another plausible explanation.
limitations: Formation-number matchups are hypotheses, not deterministic numerical outcomes; pressing assignments and player movement can erase or move an apparent spare.
Do not claim superiority, tactical intent or causation from the formation label or a short sequence.
Sparse/un-calibrated tracking and event-only data cannot establish off-ball shape, cover, or space.

cards.promptSummary: Identify the phase before the pattern: build-up vs press, progression vs block, box defence, attack after regain, or counterpress after loss. Describe the action, supporting unit, opponent response, outcome and uncertainty. These playbooks are options; apply them only when selected match evidence shows the sequence.
mechanisms: Build-up against a high press: goalkeeper and first line can create an extra passing option; pivots/8s stagger to offer forward and bounce passes; wide players stretch the press. A pass, carry, third player, switch or direct ball can bypass pressure. Risk: central turnover with defenders spread. Identify the press trigger and exits actually observed.

Progression against a mid-block: circulate to move the block, occupy distinct lines/lanes, connect a receiver between lines, or progress around/through/over the block. A full-back/winger/8 triangle can create a 2v1. Risk: sterile circulation or loss while players are ahead of the ball.

Defending the box: protect central goal-facing space, track or pass on runners according to the visible organization, contest the delivery/first contact, cover cut-back and far-post areas, then organize for the second ball. The ball source and arrival zones determine priorities; do not infer marking assignments from one frame.

Attack after a regain: first secure the ball or play forward if a safe lane and available runner are evidenced; support with width/depth and a second wave. If the direct route is closed, retain and reorganize. Risk: forcing a pass into pressure or leaving no protection after losing it again.

Counterpress after a loss: nearest player may pressure the ball, teammates can cover/screen forward outlets, and the far side may narrow. If the first pressure is bypassed, recovery toward goal can become the priority. Require the loss, pressure, cover, opponent exit and next action in sequence.

Every phase pattern includes a trigger, roles, spatial conditions, alternative action and failure mode. A coaching exercise or tactical principle describes a possible solution, not evidence that the match team selected it.
requiredEvidence: Ordered canonical events for possession changes, passes, carries, shots and outcomes, preserving source IDs/order/time.
Time-aligned tracking with validated coordinates, identities and coverage for off-ball movement, unit shape, box occupation, pressure/cover and passing options.
Phase boundaries and clock semantics; include opponent locations and relevant restarts.
analysisSteps: Classify the selected sequence and phase using canonical events; say unknown when possession/phase is uncertain.
Set the team scale: opponent block/press, ball zone, line relationships and coverage.
Trace the relevant unit and player actions in order, including supporting and covering players.
State the apparent option and the alternative/space trade-off without implying an unobserved instruction.
Follow the sequence to its evidenced outcome and state missing data.
limitations: A named phase or standard pattern cannot fill missing events/frames; do not infer off-ball roles from event-only data.
Do not label a press as successful or a progression as line-breaking without the relevant evidence.
A goal, regain or clearance after a sequence is not proof the described tactic caused it.

cards.promptSummary: Assess role fit through observed actions and support, not reputation or formation. A pivot needs safe outlets/cover; an advancing full-back needs winger/8 coordination and rest defence; a winger needs width, inside support or depth; a pressing forward needs cover behind; a target forward needs runners and second-ball support. State evidence and trade-offs.
mechanisms: Pivot: build-up angle, scanning/receiving under pressure, progression or circulation, central screening and second-ball support are distinct tasks. A pivot advancing may free a teammate to hold, but requires someone else to protect the centre.

Full-back: overlapping outside can free a winger to come inside; underlapping can occupy an inside lane while a winger holds width; staying deeper can secure rest defence. Support from an 8 or wide centre-back determines cover and return options.

Winger: holding width can stretch a block and open an inside lane; receiving inside can connect a 10/8 and free the touchline for a full-back. Both can be options, but require timing, opposite-side balance and defensive recovery.

Pressing forward: pressure angle, screening lane, trigger timing and ability of midfield/back line to step together shape whether pressure constrains an exit. Sprinting at a defender alone is not a coordinated press.

Target/central forward: securing a direct pass, setting a bounce pass, occupying centre-backs, attacking depth or contesting aerial balls are different functions. Supporting midfield runners and nearby second-ball coverage decide whether a direct outlet can be retained.
Complementarity is about task coverage, not universal player archetypes: one player may perform more than one task and duties can rotate by phase or opponent.
requiredEvidence: Validated player identity and role/lineup data; relevant event and/or time-aligned tracking evidence for the action being assessed.
Evidence of teammate support, opponent pressure and resulting space/outcome before claiming a combination helped.
Player metrics only when their definition, unit, period, sample and source quality are known.
analysisSteps: Name the task/phase rather than a personality or fixed archetype.
Identify the action observed and which teammate/opponent enables or constrains it.
State the potential benefit and the matching support/cover requirement.
Compare repeated comparable actions before describing a stable role tendency.
Describe uncertainty and avoid ranking a player without an appropriate validated evaluation model.
limitations: Do not infer speed, strength, fitness, preferred foot, aerial ability, press resistance or decision quality from a name or formation.
One successful action does not establish role suitability; results depend on teammates and opponent context.
Unknown player metrics or identities block player-specific claims.

cards.promptSummary: Treat the goalkeeper as a phase participant: build-up outlet, depth cover behind a high line, transition decision-maker and last defender. Assess passing angle, pressure, defensive line, ball/runner position and next action. Do not infer keeper height, communication or intent from events without matching evidence.
mechanisms: In build-up, the goalkeeper can widen or deepen the first line to create a safe angle and numerical option; centre-backs and pivots need staggered lanes and clear decisions to play through, around or over pressure.

When a press closes the goalkeeper, a return pass may invite pressure; the team needs a planned wide/central outlet and cover for a forced long ball. A goalkeeper pass completion alone does not establish that the press was broken.

Behind a high defensive line, goalkeeper starting depth may protect space behind defenders and allow a response to through balls. Assess ball location, opponent runners, defensive-line position, keeper position and shot/through-ball sequence together.

After a turnover, the goalkeeper can adjust toward goal/ball and communicate or organize teammates, but communication is not visible in positional/event feeds unless recorded. Covering depth and choosing whether to advance depend on attacker control, distance, angle and defender recovery.
On crosses and 1v1s, separate starting position, movement, set/ready state, decision/attempt, contact and outcome. Avoid grading the goalkeeper without a suitable shot quality/context model.
After a save/catch/restart, distribution can start a transition; its tactical value depends on teammate availability, opponent recovery and retention of the next action.
requiredEvidence: Goalkeeper identity, event/action type, event order and period/time.
Validated goalkeeper and defender/attacker locations, pitch calibration, ball location and frame coverage for depth/angle/transition claims.
For distribution assessment, destination/receiver and next possession outcome; for communication, a source that actually records it.
analysisSteps: Classify in-possession, defensive, transition or restart phase.
Locate ball, goalkeeper, defensive line, pressing attackers and available outlets if observed.
Describe the keeper action and defender support, then follow the result.
Separate measured position/action from interpretation of decision quality.
State missing views and avoid judging intent or blame.
limitations: Event-only data cannot establish starting depth, angle, body orientation, communication or positioning quality.
Do not treat the goalkeeper as automatically creating a spare player or as solely responsible for transition outcomes.
Do not apply 11-a-side conclusions to futsal/beach soccer without code-specific rules and spatial context.

cards.topic: Set-piece roles, responsibilities and second phases
cards.promptSummary: Analyze each restart separately. For corners/free kicks identify delivery, runners, blockers, edge/short options and rest defence; for defending, inspect zones/markers, first contact, clearances and outlets. Track throw-in/goal-kick options and second-ball sequence. Require event/frame evidence; never infer assignments or a foul.
mechanisms: Attacking corner: a delivery target may be combined with near/far-post, central, delayed or edge-of-box runners; blockers/screens and starting positions can alter defender sightlines. A short option can draw a defender or create a new crossing angle. Track who actually moved and where the delivery went.

Defending corner: zonal, player-to-player and hybrid structures distribute space/marking tasks differently. Inspect first-contact zones, player tracking, keeper action, edge-of-box coverage, short-corner response and the counter outlet. Do not judge a system from the goal alone.

Free kick: distinguish direct shot, cross/delivery, short combination and restart retention. Defenders may form a wall and manage runners; attackers may create decoys/blocking movements. Rules and referee decisions are canonical event/law matters, not tactical model rulings.

Throw-in: the thrower, short support, third-player option, line movement, long throw target and defensive pressure can form a local pattern. Location and restart speed matter. A long throw to the box requires first-contact, second-ball and transition-cover analysis.

Goal kick: goalkeeper, centre-backs, full-backs, pivots and forwards can form short build-up options or a direct target/second-ball structure. The opponent press determines the available route; do not assume one fixed intention.

Second phase begins after first contact/clearance: identify who regains, attacks the loose ball, protects the edge or prevents a counter. It is a new evidenced sequence, not part of an assumed routine.
Restart transition balance: retain enough players to protect central/wide counter routes while committing runners. The optimal balance is context-dependent and not inferable from formation alone.
requiredEvidence: Canonical restart type/location, source event ID/order/time, delivery/first contact/clearance/outcome and cards/fouls only if source-recorded.
Validated player identities and synchronized positions for assignments, runs, zones, first/second contact, keeper action and rest defence.
Competition/rule context for any law interpretation; the current IFAB law source takes precedence.
analysisSteps: Identify the restart and attacking/defending team; freeze selected time and event order.
Describe setup only if observed; classify marking/roles as observed or unknown.
Follow delivery, first contact, clearance and second phase separately.
Assess the next action and transition protection with evidence.
State whether the pattern is a source example or a PitchMind match observation.
limitations: Do not infer an assigned marker, blocking intent, referee decision correctness or rehearsed routine from a single outcome.
Sparse tracking may show first contact but miss off-camera runners or assignments.
Set-piece rules vary by restart and competition; tactical explanation is not a ruling on legality.

cards.promptSummary: Interpret late changes against validated score, period/clock, player count, substitutions, restart and opponent behavior. Protecting a lead, chasing a goal or playing after a dismissal may change risk and roles, but motive and causation are not proved by the state. Compare like phases and report time/source semantics.
mechanisms: Protecting a lead can involve deeper occupation, safer circulation, counter outlets, substitutions or restart management; these are alternatives, not automatic consequences. Inspect whether the block/line actually changed and whether the opponent increased pressure.

Chasing a goal can involve additional box occupation, wider/deeper runs, quicker restarts or higher defensive positioning. Additional attackers can increase attacking options while reducing cover after a turnover; report both and the observed outcome.

After a dismissal, the team with fewer players may narrow, drop a forward into midfield or preserve a counter outlet; the opponent may stretch play and overload a side. Actual shape and role changes require observed positions and the dismissal event.
An injury stoppage, substitution, penalty, corner/free kick or long throw can reset organization and change immediate risk. Separate the restart phase from open-play before/after comparisons.

Added time and “last minute” require source-specific period/time semantics. A timestamp such as 90+4 is not automatically four minutes remaining. Stoppage-time allowance and match-clock representations differ.

Late substitution evaluation should use comparable pre/post phases, define the time window, record all simultaneous changes and stop at selected time. Report association rather than causal impact unless a valid causal study exists.
Risk is multi-dimensional: exposure behind the ball, central protection, counterpress/recovery coverage, set-piece commitment and time remaining. Do not collapse it to “attacking” or “defensive”.
requiredEvidence: Canonical score, period, time semantics, dismissal/substitution/restart events and active roster at the selected time.
Time-aligned tracking/events for actual role/shape or behavior changes and opponent response.
Defined pre/post windows with sample size, phase mix, score/personnel/opponent context and all simultaneous changes.
analysisSteps: Validate time period/clock and game state; do not translate provider time to minutes remaining without documented semantics.
Identify the state change and distinguish observed fact from possible tactical response.
Compare equivalent phases/windows and list confounders or missing observations.
Describe trade-offs and outcomes only through selected-time evidence.
Use “consistent with” or “followed by” for interpretation; never assert coach motive or causal impact from sequence alone.
limitations: A late score, substitution, dismissal or foul does not reveal motive, instruction, fatigue, time-wasting intent or causality.
Small late-game samples and restart-heavy windows are not directly comparable with open-play periods.
Do not predict a result or claim a referee decision was correct from tactical context alone.

cards.topic: Shared tactical vocabulary, metric definitions and evidence confidence
cards.promptSummary: Use consistent terms; separate observation, derived metric, detector and interpretation. Compare metrics only when definitions, units, denominators, windows and coverage match. Qualify uncertainty; abstain when evidence is insufficient.
mechanisms: Distinguish possession from phase, pressure from a coordinated press, local overload from general numerical superiority, progression from penetration, and source event from tactical interpretation.
Every metric needs name/purpose, numerator, denominator, unit, aggregation window, player/team scope, provider/version, missing-data policy, sample threshold and limitations.
Keep total, per-match, per-90, per-ball-in-play, completion rate, proportion, mean, median, percentile and standard deviation distinct; incompatible denominators invalidate direct comparison.
Confidence follows source validity, identity/time mapping, calibration, coverage, sample size and definition stability; fluent wording is not evidence quality.
A general source article can support vocabulary only; it cannot support facts about the selected PitchMind match.
requiredEvidence: Evidence IDs, selected time, source revision and coverage window for match claims.
Metric definition/formula, units, denominator, scope, phase/window, provider/version and missingness for comparisons.
Validated event/player mappings and time/coordinate semantics appropriate to each claim.
analysisSteps: Label each claim as observed fact, derived measurement, detector classification or tactical interpretation.
Check metric semantics and sample comparability before interpreting or comparing values.
State coverage and plausible alternatives; choose specificity and confidence based on evidence quality.
Abstain when unknown semantics or missing observations could change the answer.
limitations: Do not compare provider metrics without confirming equivalent definitions and denominators.
Do not use model confidence or source popularity as a substitute for match evidence.
Do not label an association causal without an appropriate causal design.

cards.topic: Pressing triggers, coordination and routes out
cards.promptSummary: Treat backward pass, poor touch, touchline reception, closed orientation, slow aerial ball or isolated receiver as candidate triggers only. Check presser angle, cover shadow, supporting pressure, constrained exits, opponent response and result. Escape can go through, around, over, by carry, third player, switch or recycle. A single presser is not a team press; pressure followed by regain does not prove causation.
mechanisms: Candidate cues include backward/square pass, poor control, touchline reception, closed body orientation, slow aerial reception or isolated receiver; confirm the cue in source evidence.
Assess first presser angle and approach, cover shadow/screened lane, supporting distances, line compactness, opponent exits and next action as one sequence.
A pressing trap requires evidence that exits were constrained and the opponent responded; a touchline location alone is insufficient.
Escape routes include pass through, pass around, direct play over, bounce/third player, carry into vacated space, switch to weak side, or recycle/retain.
High pressure may win the ball near goal but risks space behind; playing through may exploit a free player but risks central turnover.
requiredEvidence: Ordered events with original IDs/times and validated possession change.
Time-aligned positions and coverage for presser/support, receiver, exits and defensive depth when coordination/shape is claimed.
Metric definitions for pressure distance/speed, trigger class or regain window if a detector supplies them.
analysisSteps: Identify the candidate cue, phase and team in possession.
Trace first pressure, cover/support, available exits and opponent response.
Classify the observed next action: regain, delay, escape, direct play, switch or recycle.
Report benefit, bypass risk and uncertainty without asserting intent or causal success.
limitations: Event-only feeds usually cannot establish body orientation, pressure, cover shadow or coordinated shape.
Do not infer a trigger, trap or collective press from one player approaching the ball.
A regain after pressure may be coincidental or caused by another action.

cards.topic: Transition phases after regain or loss
cards.promptSummary: Define transition start from a validated regain/loss and declare the end condition. Preserve source event IDs, order and clock semantics. After regain distinguish counterattack from secure possession; after loss distinguish counterpress, delay and shape recovery. Trace first action, cover, outlets, opponent recovery and outcome. Do not infer intent or causality.
mechanisms: A transition is a bounded interval after a validated possession regain or loss; state the start event and end condition such as stable possession, regain, settled block or restart.
After a regain, an immediate counterattack requires evidenced rapid forward exploitation while the opponent is disorganized; a long pass or later goal alone is insufficient.
After a loss, distinguish counterpressing, delaying the ball, protecting central access and recovering the defensive shape.
Inspect first reaction, nearest pressure, cover/screen, forward and safe outlets, opponent recovery, second action and transition protection.
If first counterpressure is bypassed, recovery runs and depth/central protection may become the next phase; use observed sequence rather than an assumed plan.
requiredEvidence: Canonical regain/loss event, original ID, sequence, period and validated time semantics.
Ordered next actions, possession state and selected-time cutoff.
Tracking coverage for pressure/support, available outlets, opponent disorganization or recovery shape claims.
analysisSteps: Fix transition start, end condition, selected time and evidence watermark.
Classify the first action and supporting/cover response.
Trace opponent reaction, next possession phase and documented outcome.
Compare rapid exploitation with secure/recovery alternatives and disclose missing coverage.
limitations: Do not call every forward pass after a regain a counterattack.
Do not label one chase as a coordinated counterpress or infer coach instruction.
Temporal order alone does not prove a press, foul or transition action caused the outcome.

cards.promptSummary: Label third-player/wall pass, overlap/underlap, switch, run behind, cutback or second ball only from defining sequences. Pair with observed defensive response. Separate pattern, chance, shot and result; outcome alone proves neither quality nor poor choice.
mechanisms: A third-player combination requires the intermediate action; an overlap runs outside/beyond the carrier; an underlap runs inside; a switch changes the attack side.
A run behind needs time-aligned starting-line and movement evidence; a cutback needs a documented delivery/location definition; a second-ball attack starts after first contact or clearance.

Possible defensive responses include screening the central lane, passing on runners, engaging/delaying the carrier, protecting depth, shifting the block, covering far-post/cutback space and contesting contact.
Trace pattern, opponent response, chance creation, shot and result as distinct stages; an outcome does not prove the earlier pattern was effective or ineffective.
Compare the attacking advantage and defensive trade-off while retaining alternatives supported by the sequence.
requiredEvidence: Ordered event IDs/times for pass, carry, delivery, first contact, shot, clearance and outcome as relevant.
Calibrated time-aligned player/ball positions and identity mapping for off-ball runs, lanes, cover or marking response.
A declared operational definition for pattern labels and chance/shot outcomes.
analysisSteps: Identify the phase and the event/positions defining the candidate pattern.
Check all required intermediate actions and local defensive cover.
Describe the defensive response and the next action through selected time.
Separate pattern, chance, shot and result; state uncertainty and alternatives.
limitations: A final cross/shot does not prove an earlier overlap, underlap, switch or third-player combination.
Do not infer assignments, deliberate blocking, decision quality or causal value from a goal alone.
Sparse event data cannot establish off-ball movement, open lanes or complete defensive coverage.

cards.promptSummary: Contextualize physical measures by role, phase, possession, minutes, period, denominator and source coverage. Keep external load (distance/speed/acceleration) separate from internal response (heart rate/perceived load). State definitions, units, method and sample; compare only compatible measures. Volume alone does not establish fatigue, effort, fitness, injury, intent or decision quality.
mechanisms: External measures may include distance, speed bands, accelerations and decelerations; internal measures may include heart-rate or perceived-load response. Do not mix constructs or infer one from another.
Interpret physical output with role, minutes played, match period, phase, possession state, score/context, sample window and tracking coverage.
Preserve raw values and denominators; normalize only with declared definitions such as per 90 minutes or per time in a relevant phase.
Measurement methods have error and coverage limits; explosive/dynamic actions may be particularly sensitive to sensor and algorithm definitions.
Compare physical and tactical observations side by side as association; require specialist validated sources for physiological/training-load claims.
requiredEvidence: Metric definition, units, device/provider/method, time window, player minutes and denominator.
Phase/possession context, role and game state, with tracking/source coverage and missingness.
For internal load, validated physiological/perceived-load source and appropriate privacy/consent controls.
analysisSteps: Separate external load, internal response and tactical event measures.
Check source quality, unit, denominator, minutes and phase context before comparison.
State association and plausible context alternatives; preserve sample and coverage limits.
Avoid causal, medical or psychological conclusions without suitable validated methods and authority.
limitations: Do not infer fatigue, effort, fitness, injury, motivation or intent from distance/sprint counts or substitution.
Incompatible devices, definitions, roles, windows and denominators do not support direct comparison.
Physical data may be sensitive personal data and requires appropriate access and governance.
